faqs.q: The term 'constitution' is derived from which Latin word?
faqs.e: Constituere literally means 'to establish or set-up'.

faqs.q: Which political scientist defined the constitution as "that body of rules or laws which determine the organization of government, the distribution of powers to the various organs of government, and the general principles on which these powers are to be exercised"?
Who defined the constitution as "the fundamental principles that determine the form of a state"?
Which scholar described the constitution as describing "the whole system of government of a country, the collection of rules which establish and regulate or govern the government"?
faqs.e: The same scholar, K.C. Wheare, later classified constitutions as rigid/flexible and described the Indian Constitution as quasi-federal.

faqs.q: Wade and Phillips defined a constitution as a document possessing which special characteristic?
Which constitutional scholar identified a comprehensive list of the functions (or purposes) of a constitution?
faqs.e: Bulmer's same framework is also the source of the procedural-prescriptive classification of constitutions.

faqs.q: According to Elliot Bulmer, which of the following is NOT one of the functions of a constitution?

options.a: It can express the identity and values of a national community
options.b: It can abolish existing political institutions of the community
options.c: It can commit states to particular social, economic, or developmental goals
options.d: It can declare and define the rights and duties of citizens

faqs.a: It can abolish existing political institutions of the community
faqs.e: Bulmer's list states a constitution can *establish and regulate* political institutions, not abolish them.

faqs.q: Which of the following is NOT among the functions of a constitution as identified by Elliot Bulmer?

options.a: It can declare and define the boundaries of the political community
options.b: It can declare and define the nature and authority of the political community
options.c: It can divide or share power between different layers of government
options.d: It can guarantee judicial review of all legislative action

faqs.a: It can guarantee judicial review of all legislative action

faqs.q: As per Elliot Bulmer's list, a constitution can declare the state's official identity in relation to which domain?
faqs.e: This function specifically covers demarcating relationships between sacred and secular authorities.

faqs.q:
Consider the following statements regarding how the constitution is described:
(I) It is described as the 'fundamental law of the land'
(II) It is described as the 'grundnorm of the country'
(III) It is described as the 'instrument of the judiciary'
Which of the above is/are correct?
faqs.e: The constitution is described as an 'instrument of the government', not the judiciary.

faqs.q: Which of the following are recognized qualities of a good constitution?

options.a: Brevity, Clarity, Definiteness and Comprehensiveness only
options.c: Brevity, Clarity, Definiteness, Comprehensiveness, Suitability, Stability and Adaptability

faqs.a: Brevity, Clarity, Definiteness, Comprehensiveness, Suitability, Stability and Adaptability
faqs.e:
The seven qualities of a good constitution are:
Brevity - precise, free of unwanted provisions.
Clarity - provisions in unambiguous terms, avoiding complicated language.
Definiteness - reduces judicial discretion by ensuring definite meaning.
Comprehensiveness - lays down both government powers and citizens' rights/duties fully.
Suitability - reflects the historical, socio-cultural, economic and political conditions of the nation.
Stability - facilitates political stability by not allowing easy tampering.
Adaptability - dynamic rather than static, functioning as a living document.

faqs.q: Constitutions are classified into which two types on the basis of evolution?
An evolved constitution, formed through conventions, practices, and judicial decisions over time, is also known as a:
Which constitution is cited as a good example of an evolved constitution?
An enacted constitution, deliberately made by a constituent assembly or promulgated by a king or parliament, is also known as a:
faqs.e: Not to be confused with 'cumulative constitution', which refers to the evolved type.

faqs.q: Constitutions are classified into which two types on the basis of incorporation of provisions?
A written constitution, consciously formulated and adopted by a constituent assembly, is also known as a:
An unwritten constitution, found in the form of conventions, practices, charters, and judicial decisions, is also known as a:

Consider the following statements regarding written constitutions:
(I) The distinction between a written and unwritten constitution is more or less the same as between an evolved and enacted constitution
(II) The USA, Canada, Japan, France and India are examples of written constitutions
(III) The UK, New Zealand and Israel are examples of written constitutions
Which of the above is/are correct?
faqs.e: UK, New Zealand and Israel are examples of unwritten constitutions, not written ones.

faqs.q: Who classified constitutions into rigid and flexible, based on the method of amendment?
A rigid constitution is one which:

options.a: Makes no distinction between constitutional and ordinary law
options.c: Cannot be amended in the same manner as ordinary laws
options.d: Can be amended in the same manner as ordinary laws

faqs.a: Cannot be amended in the same manner as ordinary laws

faqs.q: A flexible constitution, which can be amended in the same manner as ordinary laws, is also known as a:
Which country is cited as an example of a rigid (inelastic) constitution?
faqs.e: The source lists USA, Australia and Switzerland as examples of rigid constitutions.

faqs.q:
With reference to the nature of the Indian Constitution regarding rigidity and flexibility, which of the following statements is/are correct?
(I) The Indian Constitution is purely rigid
(II) The Indian Constitution is purely flexible
(III) The Indian Constitution is a synthesis of both rigid and flexible elements
Which of the above is/are correct?
Constitutions are classified into which two types on the basis of Centre-region relations?
A federal constitution is one which:

options.a: Concentrates power in the hands of the national government
options.b: Provides for a division of power between the national and regional governments
options.c: Makes regional governments subordinate agencies of the national government
options.d: Grants no independent jurisdiction to regional governments

faqs.a: Provides for a division of power between the national and regional governments

faqs.q: In a unitary constitution, the regional governments operate as:

options.b: Co-equal partners with the national government
options.c: Subordinate agencies of the national government

faqs.a: Subordinate agencies of the national government

faqs.q: Which country is cited as an example of a federal constitution?
faqs.e: USA, Switzerland, Australia, Canada, Russia and Brazil are cited as examples of federal constitutions; UK, Japan and Italy are cited as unitary examples.

faqs.q: Which scholar described the Constitution of India as 'quasi-federal'?
Elliot Bulmer classified constitutions into which two broad archetypes?
A procedural constitution primarily defines:

options.a: A broad consensus on societal goals to be achieved
options.b: The legal and political structures of public institutions and legal limits of government power
options.c: The economic and developmental targets of the state
options.d: The religious identity of the state

faqs.a: The legal and political structures of public institutions and legal limits of government power

faqs.q: A prescriptive constitution, in addition to describing how the government functions, attempts to impose:

options.b: A broad consensus on common societal goals

faqs.a: A broad consensus on common societal goals

faqs.q:
With reference to the difference between constitution and constitutionalism, consider the following statements:
(I) A country may have a constitution but not constitutionalism, as in the case of a dictatorship
(II) Constitutionalism connotes limited government and is the antithesis of arbitrary powers
(III) Constitutionalism is achieved merely by having a written constitutional document, regardless of restraints on power
Which of the above is/are correct?
faqs.e: Arbitrary power in the hands of any institution, even if conferred by a constitutional document, is a negation of constitutionalism — so a document alone does not guarantee it.

faqs.q: Constitutionalism is best described as:

options.a: A system where the executive has discretionary authority over laws
options.b: Limited government and the antithesis of arbitrary power
options.c: A synonym for a codified constitution
options.d: Unlimited government backed by a written document

faqs.a: Limited government and the antithesis of arbitrary power

faqs.q: Constitutional government, as a concept, necessarily requires the government to be:
faqs.e: The concept holds that arbitrary power in any individual or institution's hands, even under a constitutional document, negates constitutionalism, and constitutional government should necessarily be democratic.

faqs.q: The real justification of a constitution, as per the concept of constitutionalism, lies in requiring those who govern to:

options.b: Conform to laws and rules under a limited government

faqs.a: Conform to laws and rules under a limited government

faqs.q: Which scholar defined constitutionalism as providing "a system of effective restraints upon governmental action... rendering the government responsible"?
Which scholar defined constitutionalism as "essentially limited government" and "the antithesis of government by the unrestrained will of rulers"?

Which scholar stated that "constitutional government means something more than a government according to the terms of a constitution," distinguishing it from government limited only by the desires and capacities of rulers?
faqs.e: The same scholar, K.C. Wheare, also gave the classification of constitutions as rigid and unrigid (flexible) based on amendment procedure, and described India as quasi-federal.

faqs.q: Which scholar defined constitutional government as one where "the rulers are subject to a body of rules and principles, which limit the exercise of their power," describing it as the antithesis of arbitrary rule?

With reference to definitions of constitutionalism, consider the following pairs:
(I) Friedrich – System of effective restraints upon governmental action
(II) Roucek – Essentially limited government
(III) Ybema – Antithesis of arbitrary rule
Which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched?
Which scholar identified eight elements (features or principles) of constitutionalism?
faqs.e:
Henkin's eight elements are:
Popular sovereignty.
Separation of powers (checks and balances).
Government subject to the rule of law.
An independent judiciary with power of judicial review.
Civilian control of the military.
Police governed by law and subject to judicial control.
Democratic government (responsible and accountable government).
Respect for individual rights.

faqs.q:
Consider the following statements regarding elements of constitutionalism identified by Louis Henkin:
(I) Popular sovereignty
(II) Separation of powers (checks and balances)
(III) Centralised control of the police by the executive without judicial oversight
Which of the above is/are correct?
faqs.e: Henkin's list includes "police governed by law and judicial control," which is the opposite of unchecked executive control.

faqs.q: Which of the following is NOT among Louis Henkin's eight elements of constitutionalism?
Under Louis Henkin's elements of constitutionalism, control over the military should rest with:

With reference to Louis Henkin's eight elements of constitutionalism, which of the following is/are correctly included?
(I) Democratic government (responsible and accountable government)
(II) Respect for individual rights
(III) An independent judiciary
Which of the above is/are correct?
Which amendment is popularly known as the 'Mini-Constitution'?
faqs.e: The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976, made sweeping changes including adding 'socialist', 'secular', and 'integrity' to the Preamble and inserting Fundamental Duties.

faqs.q: In which landmark case did the Supreme Court rule that the constituent power of Parliament under Article 368 does not enable it to alter the 'basic structure' of the Constitution?
faqs.e: Decided in 1973, this case established the basic structure doctrine as a limitation on Parliament's amending power.

faqs.q:
Consider the following statements regarding amendments that have substantially changed the original Constitution:
(I) The 7th Amendment substantially altered original features
(II) The 97th Amendment substantially altered original features
(III) The 101st Amendment substantially altered original features
Which of the above is/are correct?
On the basis of length, the Constitution of India is classified as which type?
As originally adopted in 1949, how many Articles and Parts did the Constitution contain?
As originally adopted in 1949, how many Schedules did the Constitution contain?
Presently, the Constitution of India has about how many Articles and Parts?
Presently, how many Schedules does the Constitution have?
Which Part of the Constitution has been completely deleted through amendments since 1951?
Which of the following is among the four factors identified for the elephantine size of the Indian Constitution?

options.a: Dominance of legal luminaries in the Constituent Assembly
options.b: Absence of any foreign constitutional influence
options.c: Short duration of Constituent Assembly deliberations
options.d: Exclusion of administrative provisions from the document

faqs.a: Dominance of legal luminaries in the Constituent Assembly
faqs.e: The four factors are: geographical factors (vastness of the country and its diversity); historical factors (influence of the Government of India Act of 1935); dominance of legal luminaries in the Constituent Assembly; and a single Constitution for both the Centre and the states (not multiple separate constitutions).

faqs.q: Till 2019, J&K's special status was under which Article of the Constitution?
J&K's special status was abolished in 2019 through a presidential order officially known as:

options.a: The Constitution (Application to Jammu and Kashmir) Order, 1954
options.b: The Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Order, 2019
options.c: The Constitution (Application to Jammu and Kashmir) Order, 2019
options.d: The Jammu and Kashmir Special Status Repeal Order, 2019

faqs.a: The Constitution (Application to Jammu and Kashmir) Order, 2019
faqs.e: This 2019 order superseded the earlier 1954 order of the same broader title and extended all provisions of the Constitution of India to Jammu and Kashmir.

faqs.q: The J&K Reorganisation Act, 2019 bifurcated J&K into which two Union territories?
Who acclaimed that the Constitution was framed after 'ransacking all the known Constitutions of the World'?

With reference to the sources of different parts of the Indian Constitution, consider the following pairs:

(II) Philosophical part – American and Irish Constitutions respectively
(III) Political part – British Constitution
Which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched?

faqs.e: The Federal Scheme, Judiciary, Governors, Emergency Powers, Public Service Commissions, and most administrative details are drawn from this Act, with more than half of the Constitution's provisions closely resembling it.

faqs.q: Constitutions are classified into rigid and flexible on the basis of which criterion?
Which country is cited as an example of a rigid constitution requiring a special amendment procedure?
As per Article 368, some provisions of the Indian Constitution can be amended by a special majority of Parliament along with which additional requirement?

options.b: Ratification by half of the total states

faqs.a: Ratification by half of the total states
faqs.e: This applies to provisions affecting the federal structure, such as election of the President and distribution of legislative powers.

faqs.q: Which type of Constitutional amendment under Article 368 requires a two-third majority of members present and voting, along with a majority of the total membership of each House?
faqs.e:
A third category — provisions amendable by a simple majority in the manner of ordinary legislative process — also exists and falls outside the scope of Article 368.

faqs.q: The Constitution of India establishes which system of government based on the relationship between the national and regional governments?

faqs.q: Which of the following is a unitary (non-federal) feature found in the Indian Constitution?

options.c: Appointment of state governor by the Centre

faqs.a: Appointment of state governor by the Centre

faqs.q: Which Article uses the term 'Union of States' instead of 'Federation' for India?
faqs.e: Article 1 describes India as a 'Union of States', a term nowhere replaced by the word 'Federation' anywhere in the Constitution.

faqs.q: Article 1 of the Constitution describes India as a:

Which of the above is/are correct?

faqs.q: India adopted the British Parliamentary System rather than which alternative system?

faqs.e: In contrast, the presidential system is based on the doctrine of separation of powers between the two organs.

faqs.e: Westminster is the place in London where the British Parliament is located, and the term is often used as a symbol or synonym for it.

faqs.q:

(II) Membership of ministers in the legislature
(III) Fixed tenure of the lower House with no provision for dissolution
Which of the above is/are correct?
faqs.e: Dissolution of the lower House (Lok Sabha or Assembly) is itself one of the listed features of parliamentary government, contradicting the idea of a fixed tenure with no dissolution.

faqs.q: Which of the following is a fundamental difference between the Indian and British parliamentary systems?

options.a: Britain has a bicameral legislature while India does not
options.b: India has a nominal executive while Britain does not
options.c: India follows collective responsibility while Britain does not
options.d: The Indian Parliament is not a sovereign body unlike the British Parliament

faqs.a: The Indian Parliament is not a sovereign body unlike the British Parliament

faqs.q: With reference to differences between the Indian and British states, which of the following is correct regarding their heads of state?

options.c: India has a hereditary head while Britain has an elected head
options.d: India has an elected head while Britain has a hereditary head

faqs.a: India has an elected head while Britain has a hereditary head
faqs.e: India is a republic, while Britain remains a monarchy.

faqs.q: In a parliamentary system, whether in India or Britain, the significant and crucial role of which office has led political scientists to call it a 'Prime Ministerial Government'?

options.b: Due process of law versus procedure established by law
options.d: Rule of law versus due process

faqs.a: Due process of law versus procedure established by law
faqs.e: The American Constitution provides for 'due process of law', while the Indian Constitution under Article 21 provides for 'procedure established by law', which is narrower in scope.

faqs.q: 'Procedure established by law' is contained in which Article?

options.b: British parliamentary sovereignty and American judicial supremacy

options.b: Two parallel and separate systems of courts
options.c: State-level courts alone, with no central oversight
options.d: A single integrated system of courts headed by the Supreme Court

faqs.a: A single integrated system of courts headed by the Supreme Court

faqs.q:
Consider the following statements regarding provisions ensuring the independence of the Supreme Court:
(I) Security of tenure of the judges
(II) All expenses of the Supreme Court charged on the Consolidated Fund of India
(III) Unrestricted power of the legislature to discuss the conduct of judges
Which of the above is/are correct?
faqs.e: There is actually a prohibition on discussion of the conduct of judges in the legislatures, which is itself one of the safeguards ensuring judicial independence.

faqs.q: Part III of the Constitution presently guarantees how many fundamental rights?

(II) They are absolute and admit of no restrictions whatsoever
(III) They can be curtailed or repealed by Parliament through a Constitutional Amendment Act
Which of the above is/are correct?
faqs.e: Fundamental Rights are not absolute and are subject to reasonable restrictions, so statement II is incorrect.

faqs.q: During the operation of a National Emergency, Fundamental Rights can be suspended except those guaranteed under which Articles?

An aggrieved person whose fundamental rights are violated can directly approach the Supreme Court, which can issue writs for the restoration of rights. Which of the following is NOT one of these writs?
faqs.e: The five writs available are habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, and quo warranto.

faqs.q: According to Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, the Directive Principles of State Policy represent which kind of feature of the Indian Constitution?

options.c: Enforceable only against the Union government

faqs.q: In which landmark case did the Supreme Court hold that 'the Indian Constitution is founded on the bedrock of the balance between the Fundamental Rights and the Directive Principles'?
faqs.e: Decided in 1980, this case reinforced the idea that neither Fundamental Rights nor Directive Principles can be given absolute primacy over the other.

faqs.q: The original Constitution of India, as adopted, did not provide for which of the following?
Fundamental Duties were added by which Amendment Act?
faqs.e: Fundamental Duties were added during the internal emergency of 1975-77, on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee. They are contained in Part IV-A, Article 51-A. The 86th Amendment Act later added one more Fundamental Duty to the original list.

faqs.q: Like the Directive Principles of State Policy, the Fundamental Duties are:

options.d: Enforceable only during a National Emergency

faqs.q: The term 'secular' was added to the Preamble by which Amendment Act?

options.c: Reservation of seats for scheduled castes and scheduled tribes

faqs.a: Reservation of seats in the legislatures on the basis of religion

faqs.q: Despite abolishing communal representation, the Constitution provides for the temporary reservation of seats for which groups to ensure adequate representation?
Universal adult franchise is the basis for elections to which bodies?

options.c: The Lok Sabha and the state legislative assemblies

faqs.q: Under universal adult franchise, what is the minimum voting age?
The voting age was reduced from 21 to 18 by which Amendment Act?
faqs.e: This amendment, passed in 1988, brought the voting age down to 18 years starting from 1989.

options.d: Neither the national nor the state government

How many types of emergencies does the Indian Constitution envisage?
faqs.e: The three types of emergencies are: National Emergency (Article 352); State Emergency/President's Rule for failure of constitutional machinery (Article 356); and Financial Emergency (Article 360).

The 74th Amendment Act of 1992 added which new Part and Schedule to the Constitution?

faqs.a: An extra-constitutional declaration not affecting India's sovereignty

faqs.q: Being a sovereign state, India has the constitutional capacity to:

options.a: Only cede territory, never acquire any
options.b: Both acquire a foreign territory and cede a part of its own territory
options.c: Only acquire foreign territory, never cede any
options.d: Neither acquire nor cede any territory

faqs.a: Both acquire a foreign territory and cede a part of its own territory

faqs.q: Even before the term 'socialist' was formally added to the Preamble, the Constitution already carried socialist content in the form of which provisions?
In which year and at which session did the Congress party adopt a resolution to establish a 'socialistic pattern of society'?

Consider the following statements regarding the nature of Indian socialism:
(I) It represents 'democratic socialism' rather than 'communistic socialism'
(II) It involves the nationalisation of all means of production and abolition of private property
(III) It holds faith in a 'mixed economy' where public and private sectors co-exist
Which of the above is/are correct?
faqs.e: Nationalisation of all means of production and abolition of private property describes 'communistic socialism' or 'state socialism', which Indian socialism is explicitly distinguished from.

faqs.q: Which 1991 economic policy is noted to have diluted the socialist credentials of the Indian State?

options.a: The policy of liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation

faqs.a: The policy of liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation

faqs.q: The term 'secular' was added to the Preamble by which Amendment Act?

In 1974, the Supreme Court observed that although the words 'secular state' were not expressly mentioned in the Constitution, the intent to establish such a state was reflected through which Articles?
The Indian Constitution embodies which concept of secularism, under which all religions in the country have the same status and support from the state?
On the basis of the state's attitude towards religion, a state that is anti-religion and condemns all religions is classified as:
A state that declares one particular religion as the state religion is classified as:
faqs.e: Bangladesh, Burma, Sri Lanka and Pakistan are cited as examples of theocratic states, while USA and India are cited as examples of secular states.

faqs.q: The term 'democratic' in the Preamble is based on which doctrine?
In which type of democracy do the people exercise their supreme power directly, as is the case in Switzerland?
Which of the following is NOT one of the four devices of direct democracy?
faqs.e: The four devices of direct democracy are Referendum, Initiative, Recall and Plebiscite.

faqs.q: Which device of direct democracy refers to a procedure whereby a proposed legislation is referred to the electorate for settlement by their direct votes?
Which device of direct democracy allows people to propose a bill to the legislature for enactment?
Which device of direct democracy allows voters to remove a representative or officer before the expiry of their term for failing to discharge duties properly?
Which device of direct democracy is generally used to obtain the opinion of people on an issue of public importance, especially to solve territorial disputes?
Indirect democracy is also known as:
Representative democracy is of two kinds. Which of the following correctly identifies them?

Who stressed the dimension of social democracy in his concluding speech in the Constituent Assembly on November 25, 1949, stating that "political democracy cannot last unless there lies at the base of it social democracy"?
In a monarchy, the head of the state comes to office through which method, as exemplified by Britain?
The term 'republic' in the Preamble indicates that the President is:

options.a: A hereditary position like a monarch
options.b: Elected indirectly for a fixed period
options.d: Elected directly by universal adult franchise

faqs.a: Elected indirectly for a fixed period

faqs.q: The President of India is elected indirectly for a fixed term of how many years?

Consider the following statements regarding the implications of the term 'republic' in the Preamble:
(I) It vests political sovereignty in the people, not in a single individual like a king
(II) It implies the absence of any privileged class, with public offices open to every citizen
(III) It requires the head of state to always be elected directly by the people
Which of the above is/are correct?
faqs.e: A republic requires the head of state to be elected, but not necessarily directly, since the term embraces both direct and indirect election, as with India's indirectly elected President.

faqs.q: The term 'justice' in the Preamble embraces how many distinct forms?
Which form of justice denotes the equal treatment of all citizens without any social distinction based on caste, colour, race, religion or sex?
Which form of justice involves the elimination of glaring inequalities in wealth, income and property?
A combination of social justice and economic justice is together known as:
Which form of justice implies that all citizens should have equal political rights, equal access to political offices and equal voice in government?
The ideal of justice in the Preamble has been taken from which historical event?
faqs.e: The Russian Revolution took place in 1917, while the ideals of liberty, equality and fraternity were taken from the French Revolution (1789-1799).

faqs.q: The term 'liberty' in the Preamble means:

options.a: Freedom limited only to political expression
options.b: Absence of restraints on individual activities along with opportunities for personal development
options.c: Freedom exercised without any Constitutional limitations
options.d: Complete license to do whatever one likes without restraint

faqs.a: Absence of restraints on individual activities along with opportunities for personal development

faqs.q: The ideals of liberty, equality and fraternity in the Preamble have been taken from which historical event?
As elaborated in the Preamble, is the liberty conceived by the Preamble or the fundamental rights absolute or qualified?

options.b: Qualified, subject to limitations mentioned in the Constitution
options.c: Applicable only to citizens above 21 years of age

faqs.a: Qualified, subject to limitations mentioned in the Constitution

faqs.q: The term 'equality' in the Preamble embraces how many dimensions?
Which of the following correctly identifies the three dimensions of equality embraced by the Preamble?

Consider the following statements regarding provisions of the Fundamental Rights chapter that ensure civic equality:
(I) Equality before the law under Article 14
(II) Abolition of untouchability under Article 17
(III) Equal pay for equal work under Article 39
Which of the above is/are correct?
faqs.e: Equal pay for equal work under Article 39 is a Directive Principle of State Policy securing economic equality, not a civic equality provision under the Fundamental Rights chapter.

faqs.q: Which Article bars exclusion from electoral rolls on grounds of religion, race, caste or sex?
Which Article provides for Lok Sabha and state assembly elections on adult suffrage?
Which DPSP Article secures equal right to livelihood and equal pay for equal work?
The Constitution promotes the feeling of fraternity primarily through which system?
The Preamble declares that fraternity has to assure which two things?

options.a: Dignity of the individual and unity and integrity of the nation
options.b: Equality and dignity of the individual

faqs.a: Dignity of the individual and unity and integrity of the nation

faqs.q: The word 'integrity' was added to the Preamble by which Amendment Act?
According to K.M. Munshi, the phrase 'dignity of the individual' signifies that the Constitution recognises that:

options.a: The State has absolute authority over individual personality
options.b: Only citizens with property rights possess dignity
options.c: Dignity applies only to elected representatives
options.d: The personality of every individual is sacred

faqs.a: The personality of every individual is sacred

faqs.q: Article 1 of the Constitution describes India as a 'Union of States' in order to make clear that:

options.a: States can unilaterally alter their boundaries
options.b: States have the right to secede from the Union
options.c: States can form their own separate constitutions
options.d: States have no right to secede from the Union

faqs.a: States have no right to secede from the Union
faqs.e: This implies the indestructible nature of the Indian Union and reinforces the phrase 'unity and integrity of the nation' in the Preamble.

faqs.q: Who said, "The Preamble to our Constitution expresses what we had thought or dreamt so long"?
According to K.M. Munshi, the Preamble is the:

Which member of the Constituent Assembly described the Preamble as "the most precious part of the Constitution... the soul of the Constitution... a key to the Constitution... a jewel set in the Constitution"?
Which distinguished English political scientist described the Preamble as the 'key-note' to the Constitution and quoted it at the opening of his book "Principles of Social and Political Theory"?

Which former Chief Justice of India observed that the Preamble "resembles the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America, but is more than a declaration... It contains a solemn resolve, which nothing but a revolution can alter"?
In which case did the Supreme Court first hold that the Preamble is not part of the Constitution?
In the Berubari Union case (1960), the Supreme Court held that where the terms used in any article are ambiguous or capable of more than one meaning, assistance at interpretation may be taken from:

options.a: The Directive Principles of State Policy
options.b: The objectives enshrined in the Preamble

faqs.a: The objectives enshrined in the Preamble

faqs.q: In which case did the Supreme Court hold that the Preamble is part of the Constitution?
Besides Kesavananda Bharati, in which other case did the Court hold the Preamble is an integral part of the Constitution?

Consider the following statements regarding the enactment and status of the Preamble:
(I) The Preamble was enacted by the Constituent Assembly after the rest of the Constitution was already enacted
(II) The reason for inserting the Preamble at the end was to ensure conformity with the Constitution as adopted
(III) The President of the Constituent Assembly stated that the Preamble does not stand as part of the Constitution
Which of the above is/are correct?
faqs.e: The President of the Constituent Assembly actually said, 'The question is that Preamble stands part of the Constitution', and this motion was adopted.

faqs.q: Regarding the Preamble's legal standing, which of the following is correct?

options.a: It is a prohibition upon the powers of the legislature
options.b: It is a source of power to the legislature
options.c: It overrides all other provisions of the Constitution
options.d: It is neither a source of power to the legislature nor a prohibition upon its powers

faqs.a: It is neither a source of power to the legislature nor a prohibition upon its powers

faqs.q: The Preamble is non-justiciable, which means:

options.a: It requires ratification by the states
options.b: It applies only to the Union government
options.c: Its provisions are not enforceable in courts of law
options.d: It cannot be amended under any circumstances

faqs.a: Its provisions are not enforceable in courts of law

faqs.q: The question of whether the Preamble can be amended under Article 368 arose for the first time in which case?
In the Kesavananda Bharati case, the Supreme Court held that the Preamble can be amended subject to which condition?

options.a: No amendment can be made without a national referendum
options.b: No amendment can be done to the 'basic features' of the Constitution
options.c: Amendments require the consent of all state legislatures
options.d: The Preamble can never be amended under any condition

faqs.a: No amendment can be done to the 'basic features' of the Constitution

faqs.q: As of now, how many times has the Preamble been amended?
faqs.e: The Preamble was amended only once, in 1976, by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, and this amendment was held to be valid.
